newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. and Japan reach final deal on insurance.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and Japan reach final deal on insurance.

text.p: Japan and the United States have reached final agreement on a deal to open up Japan's $400 billion insurance market to greater international competition, the U.S. embassy said in a statement on Sunday.
It hailed the accord, saying it will "allow foreign companies to compete more effectively and provide Japanese consumers with a greater choice of innovative products and lower prices."
Japan had said late Saturday that a basic agreement had been worked out between Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky and Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka.
The deal will deregulate Japan's primary life, property and casualty insurance markets, in which foreign firms have a negligible share.

It also delays the entry of Japan's major insurance groups into some sectors of the so-called "third market" in which foreign companies have gained a foothold. This sector includes specialty coverage such as cancer, travel and accident insurance.
The two countries had agreed on an insurance accord in 1994 but the United States objected to the manner in which it was being implemented, saying it favoured Japanese companies.

U.S. President Bill Clinton had called the dispute the largest trade issue between the two economic superpowers and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto had expressed relief on news of the tentative accord on Saturday.
